text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Danish tax minister Carsten Koch is to stop tax exemption for funds used by firms for bribing officials to win orders in developing and Far Eastern countries, where such customs are rife. Koch plans to get Sweden and Finland to abolish these tax deductions as well in a joint Nordic effort to fight corrupt business practices. Norway has already done so.

--Former German chancellor Helmut Schmidt predicts that Denmark and Sweden will be queueing up to join EMU (Europe's economic and monetary union) when it becomes a final reality in the year 2002. Schmidt says the advantages for business will be so overwhelmingly obvious that both Danish and Swedish industry and ordinary citizens will pressure governments to join five years after a common European currency is introduced at the latest.

--Following serious criticism, Copenhagen Stock Exchange is soon to start issuing mid-session and closing bond and share prices on Internet, with on-line whole day rates to be available eventually to subscribers for a monthly subscription of around 200 crowns.
--State early pension schemes remain popular in Denmark with 1,200 more going into premature retirement so far this year, bringing the total to 127,500 as foreseen in the 1997 state budget.

--British-German investment bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) warns of possible overheating of the Danish economy in a new report. It said the strength of the Danish economic upturn meant that Denmark's Central Bank might have to raise interest rates this year or early next year, before the Bundesbank does so. DMG has upwardly adjusted its forecast for Danish GDP growth this year to 3.1 percent from 2.8 percent.
